title: Sorting Results with ORDER BY 🔃
description: Order your query results ascending or descending by one or multiple columns.

slides.title: Why Sort? 📊
slides.content:
# Bring Order to Your Results

SQL tables don’t guarantee any row order unless you explicitly sort. Use `ORDER BY` to control the output sequence.

```sql
SELECT * FROM employees ORDER BY salary;
```

By default, sorting is **ascending** (smallest to largest).

slides.title: Basic ORDER BY
slides.codeSnippet: SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary;

quizData.question: What is the default sort order of `ORDER BY column`?

slides.title: Descending Order 🔽
slides.content:
## Use `DESC`

Add `DESC` (descending) after the column name:

```sql
SELECT * FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC;
```

Now highest salary comes first.

You can explicitly write `ASC` for ascending, but it’s the default.

slides.title: Sort Descending
slides.codeSnippet: SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC;

slides.title: Sorting by Multiple Columns 📑
slides.content:
## Tie‑Breaking

If two rows have the same value in the first sort column, you can specify a second column:

```sql
SELECT * FROM employees ORDER BY department ASC, salary DESC;
```

This sorts by department alphabetically, and within each department, by salary descending.

Separate column names with commas, each with its own `ASC`/`DESC`.

slides.title: Multi‑Column Sort
slides.content: Order by department then salary descending:

quizData.question: What does `ORDER BY col1 DESC, col2 ASC` do?

options.text: Sorts by col1 descending; where col1 ties, sorts by col2 ascending
Sorts by col1 ascending, then col2 descending

quizData.explanation: The first column takes precedence; subsequent columns break ties.

slides.title: Sorting with Expressions and Aliases 📐
slides.content:
## You Can Sort by Calculated Values

```sql
SELECT name, salary * 1.1 AS adjusted_salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY adjusted_salary DESC;
```

You can also sort by column position (ordinal), e.g., `ORDER BY 2 DESC`, but that’s brittle. Prefer column names.

slides.title: Sort by Expression
slides.codeSnippet: SELECT name, salary, salary * 1.1 AS bonus FROM employees ORDER BY bonus DESC;

quizData.question: Can you use `ORDER BY 2` to sort by the second column in the SELECT list?

options.text: Yes, it refers to the position
It means sort by the constant 2

quizData.explanation: Ordinal positions are allowed but considered bad practice because they break if columns are re‑ordered.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## NULLS in Sorting

By default, NULLs appear at the beginning in SQLite for ascending order. Use `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST` in PostgreSQL; SQLite doesn’t support that but you can work around it.

slides.title: Sort Challenge 🏋️
slides.content:
Write queries:
1. List all employees sorted by name alphabetically.
2. List employees from Sales first, then by salary descending.
3. Show name and a 5% raise as `new_salary`, and sort by that new salary descending.

Use the `employees` table.

slides.title: Sorting Complete! 🎉
slides.content: You can now retrieve and order data exactly how you want. In the next chapter, we’ll dive deeper into advanced filtering and aggregations.
